transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lynda Kenyon.
The House is moving toward a procedural vote later today on articles of impeachment against
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
As NPR's Tom Bowman reports, the impeachment effort is led by Kentucky Representative Thomas
Massey.
He's basically saying Hegseth went to war without getting congressional approval, went
to war with Iran, the same with Yemen, didn't get congressional approval, and also the attacks
on the alleged drug boats in the Caribbean, also without congressional approval.
He said there's been a disregard for civilian casualties in Iran.
Remember, there was that U.S. strike on a girls' school that killed up to 150 or so
people.
Another on a sports complex killed 20 or so.
In his first news conference in six months, Secretary Hegseth called the impeachment proceedings
a political spectacle.
On social media, President Trump said he gives Hegseth's performance an A+++.
A California proposition to establish a first-in-the-nation wealth tax has failed.
That's according to a race call by the Associated Press.
KQED's Laura Fitzgerald has the story.
California's Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% wealth tax on the state's billionaires.
Around 53% of voters opposed it.
Prop 40 was backed by a health care workers' union, and most of the revenue would have
been used to fund health care.
Opponents, including Governor Gavin Newsom, said the tax would ultimately hurt the state's
budget.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin funneled over $100 million into two measures designed to
cancel out the wealth tax.
For NPR News, I'm Laura Fitzgerald in San Francisco.
Exxon has signed a preliminary agreement with Venezuela's government that could help bring
the American company's return to that nation's oil fields and begin to produce oil for the
American markets.
Manuel Ruedo reports from Caracas.
Exxon described the memorandum of understanding signed Monday night as a meaningful first
step but warned that future investments will depend on clear regulations and strong investment
protections.
In 2007, Exxon had billions of dollars worth of assets seized by Venezuela's socialist
government after the company refused to comply with a reform that forced foreign companies
to become minority partners in Venezuela's oil fields.
But much has changed in Venezuela since U.S. troops removed President Nicolás Maduro in
January.
The new administration is providing more generous terms to oil companies and has already cut
deals with companies backed by Washington for NPR News and Manuel Ruedo in Caracas.
Exxon says it plans to evaluate drilling opportunities in Venezuela in the coming months.
At last check on Wall Street, the Dow was down 230 points.
The S&P 500 was down 48.
You're listening to NPR.
Editors and publishers say they're being inundated with AI-generated submissions.
Some are turning to detection tools to differentiate between human writing and chatbots.
But as NPR's Windsor Johnston reports, those tools do not always get it right.
The flood of suspected writing generated by AI means more work for editors.
Neil Clark is the publisher of the science fiction magazine Clark's World.
It's adding so much to our workload.
I know that mine is increased by 25 to 30 percent.
AI detectors look for patterns in language.
Chris Callison Burch is an artificial intelligence expert at the University of Pennsylvania.
Adverbs like notably or crucially at the beginning of sentences are often AI writing or things
that are self-posed rhetorical questions.
But people use those word patterns, too, so human writing can get flagged as AI.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
A new study suggests reducing air pollution to the guidelines set by the World Health
Organization could save more than nine million lives a year.
The study, published in the journal Environment International, estimates meeting those guidelines
could most benefit low and middle income countries, where deaths from heart disease and stroke
are strongly linked to air pollution.
Over 90 percent of the global population currently lives in places that do not meet the current
guidelines set by the World Health Organization.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: House moves toward procedural vote on impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Hegseth calls impeachment proceedings a political spectacle; Trump gives him an A+++
California Proposition 40 wealth tax on billionaires fails, per AP race call
Exxon signs preliminary agreement with Venezuela's government to return to oil fields
Editors report AI-generated submission floods; detection tools prone to false flags
Study says meeting WHO air pollution guidelines could save over nine million lives yearly
